content: Chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a gonadotropin hormone approved by the FDA for specific medical conditions. It is used to treat prepubertal cryptorchidism not caused by anatomical obstruction, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in males, and to induce ovulation and pregnancy in anovulatory infertile women who have been pretreated with human menotropins. It is not effective as adjunctive therapy for obesity, as there is no substantial evidence that it promotes weight loss beyond caloric restriction, redistributes fat, or reduces hunger associated with calorie-restricted diets. For prepubertal cryptorchidism, hCG is thought to induce testicular descent in cases where descent would have occurred at puberty. However, the response is often temporary, and therapy is typically initiated between ages 4 and 9. Dosage regimens vary, including 4,000 USP units three times weekly for three weeks or 500 USP units three times weekly for four to six weeks. If the initial course is unsuccessful, another course may be started one month later with adjusted dosages. In males with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, hCG is administered at doses such as 500 to 1,000 USP units three times weekly for three weeks, followed by the same dose twice weekly for three weeks. Alternatively, 4,000 USP units three times weekly for six to nine months may be used, with a reduced dose of 2,000 USP units three times weekly for an additional three months. For anovulatory infertile women, hCG is given at 5,000 to 10,000 USP units one day after the last dose of menotropins. A dose of 10,000 USP units is recommended in the labeling for menotropins. hCG is contraindicated in cases of precocious puberty, prostatic carcinoma, or other androgen-dependent neoplasms, as well as in individuals with a prior allergic reaction to hCG. It may cause fetal harm if administered to pregnant women. Combined hCG and pregnant mare's serum (PMS) therapy has been associated with a high incidence of external congenital anomalies in mice, though the relevance to humans is unclear. Warnings include the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, which can cause sudden ovarian enlargement, ascites, and pleural effusion. Other risks include enlargement or rupture of preexisting ovarian cysts, multiple births, and arterial thromboembolism. Anaphylaxis has been reported with urinary-derived hCG products. Benzyl alcohol, a component of some formulations, has been associated with fatal gasping syndrome in premature infants. Adverse reactions include headache, irritability, restlessness, depression, fatigue, edema, precocious puberty, gynecomastia, and injection site pain. Hypersensitivity reactions, both localized and systemic, such as erythema, urticaria, rash, angioedema, and dyspnea, have been reported. The relationship of these reactions to the hormone or the diluent containing benzyl alcohol is unclear. hCG is administered intramuscularly, and parenteral drug products should be inspected for particulate matter and discoloration before use. Used needles and syringes should be disposed of in a puncture-resistant sharps container and taken to an appropriate collection center for disposal. In some states, it is illegal to dispose of medical sharps in household garbage. hCG mimics the action of luteinizing hormone (LH) and has some follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) activity. It stimulates gonadal steroid hormone production by acting on Leydig cells in the testes to produce androgens and on the corpus luteum in the ovary to produce progesterone. In males, androgen stimulation leads to the development of secondary sexual characteristics and may stimulate testicular descent if no anatomical obstruction is present. In females, hCG can substitute for LH to trigger ovulation during the menstrual cycle. hCG has no known effect on fat mobilization, appetite, hunger, or body fat distribution. It is a water-soluble glycoprotein derived from human pregnancy urine and is composed of alpha and beta subunits. The alpha subunit is identical to that of human pituitary gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), while the beta subunit differs in amino acid sequence. The drug should be stored as a dry product at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F), with excursions permitted between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). Once reconstituted, the solution should be refrigerated and used within 30 days. Each vial contains 10,000 USP units of hCG, along with mannitol, dibasic sodium phosphate, and monobasic sodium phosphate. There is limited information regarding hCG's pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, nonclinical toxicology, and clinical studies in the drug label. It is not known whether hCG is excreted in human milk, and safety and effectiveness in children under 4 years of age have not been established. There is no FDA guidance on its use in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or those with renal or hepatic impairment. Additionally, there is no established interaction between hCG and alcohol. The brand name for hCG is Novarel®.
